label: Compatible Triples
notes: This short lecture spans printed pages 72 through 75. The aim is to stop treating the symplectic form, the almost complex structure, and the metric as three separate gadgets. Once compatibility holds, they form one package in which any two of the three reconstruct the missing one.

label: The Three Structures
notes: Set the stage by naming the three players: a nondegenerate two-form omega, an almost complex structure J squaring to minus one, and a Riemannian metric g. Each lives in its own world, yet the lecture will tie them together by a single bilinear identity that links all three at once.

label: The Binding Identity
notes: The whole lecture pivots on one formula, g of u and v equals omega of u and J v. Compatibility means this g is symmetric and positive definite. Stress that this single equation is the bridge: it converts the antisymmetric omega into the symmetric g using J as the twist.

label: Any Two Determine the Third
notes: Walk the triangle. Given omega and J, define g by the identity. Given g and J, recover omega through omega of u and v equals g of J u and v. Given omega and g, polar decomposition extracts J. The point is closure: no vertex is independent of the other two.

label: Compatibility Conditions
notes: Spell out what compatibility actually demands. The form must tame J, meaning omega of v and J v is positive for nonzero v, and J must preserve omega. Together these give a genuine inner product. Emphasize that positivity, not mere nondegeneracy, is what makes the metric usable.

label: J Is an Isometry
notes: Show that compatibility forces J to be orthogonal for g, that is J transpose g J equals g. So J rotates each tangent space by ninety degrees while preserving lengths. This orthogonality is the linear-algebra heart of why the triple behaves like multiplication by i on a Hermitian space.

label: Analogy with C-n
notes: Anchor intuition in the model. On complex n-space the Hermitian form splits into a real symmetric part, the metric, and an imaginary antisymmetric part, the symplectic form, joined by multiplication by i. The compatible triple on a manifold is exactly this Hermitian package carried pointwise on tangent spaces.

label: Reduction to U(n)
notes: Explain the structure-group payoff. A bare tangent bundle has frames related by the full linear group. Asking frames to respect omega, J, and g simultaneously forces transitions into the unitary group, the common intersection of the symplectic, complex-linear, and orthogonal groups. The triple is a U(n) structure.

label: The Space of Compatible J
notes: State the existence and contractibility theorem. For any symplectic form the space of compatible almost complex structures is nonempty and contractible. Contractibility is stronger than connectedness: it means the space deformation retracts to a point, so no topological choice is hidden in picking a J.

label: Why Contractibility Matters
notes: Draw the consequence for invariants. Because the choice of compatible J is contractible, any invariant built using an auxiliary J cannot depend on which J was chosen. This licenses Chern classes and almost-complex machinery as honest symplectic invariants, defined up to the contractible ambiguity.

label: A Deformation Caution
notes: Separate two statements that are easy to conflate. If two symplectic forms share a compatible J, their convex path stays symplectic because the induced metrics stay positive. But a path of symplectic forms alone does not force one common compatible J; the standard four-dimensional example shows the converse fails.

label: Recap
notes: Gather the threads. One identity links omega, J, and g; any two determine the third; J becomes a g-isometry; the structure group drops to U(n); and the space of compatible J is contractible, so auxiliary almost complex structures yield genuine symplectic invariants. This is the toolkit for the rest of the course.
